findings.claim: Thirty-two practice questions across all eight lessons are labelled “20 marks — Extract Analysis”, and ten more “40 marks — 19th Century Essay”.
findings.truth: Section B on the 19th-century prose text is ONE source-based question worth 40 marks, with an extract printed on the paper. There is no 20-mark part and no separate essay question. All 48 questions relabelled “40 marks — Extract Analysis”.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md — “Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks) … through a source based response”.

findings.claim: Mark ladders run “Top band (9–10) … Lower band (1–2)” or “Top band (4–5) … Lower band (1)”.
findings.truth: Ladders rescaled to the 40-mark house ladder: Top band (33–40) / Upper-mid band (25–32) / Mid band (17–24) / Lower-mid band (9–16) / Low band (1–8), matching the sibling Eduqas 19th-century units.
findings.evidence: Section B is a single 40-mark question; house ladder as used in english-literature-eduqas__war-of-the-worlds and __jane-eyre.

findings.claim: Ten mark schemes read “AO1 (up to 10) … AO2 (up to 10) … AO3 (up to 10) … AO4 (up to 10): Accurate spelling, punctuation, grammar”.
findings.truth: Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 only. AO4 does not exist on this question, so spelling and grammar earn no marks; the spec also states no numeric split of the 40 marks between objectives. Schemes rebuilt on the house ladder with three objectives.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md — “Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.” (AO4 belongs to Section A only).

findings.claim: The board is named in student-facing text in lessons 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 — including “the Eduqas C720U Component 2, Section B exam” (L1), “For the Eduqas C720U exam” (L7), the L6 and L8 lesson descriptions, and a knowledge-check stem in L8.
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board or its spec codes. Reworded to “the exam” / “the 19th-century novel question”.
findings.evidence: House rule (feedback_eduqas_wjec_neutral_phrasing); same fix applied across the sibling Eduqas units.

findings.claim: “Context (AO3) is worth up to 10 of the 40 marks.”
findings.truth: The specification gives no numeric split of the 40 marks between AO1, AO2 and AO3. Reworded to say context is one of the three objectives assessed on the 40-mark question.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md — Section B states the objectives but no per-AO mark allocation.

findings.claim: “Eliot describes the gold as his ‘companions’” — repeated in a knowledge-check answer option, a flashcard and a mark scheme.
findings.truth: Eliot does not call the coins “companions”. Chapter 2 reads that Silas drew them out “to enjoy their companionship”, and the coins “had become his familiars”. The only “companion” in the novel is Silas’s brown earthenware pot.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text ch. 2: “those coins, which had become his familiars”; “that he drew them out to enjoy their companionship”; ch. 2: “It had been his companion for twelve years” (the water pot).

findings.claim: Flashcards state that Dunstan enters because “the door is left open while Silas is having a cataleptic fit”, and that Silas is in a cataleptic fit during the theft.
findings.truth: Silas has walked to the village to fetch twine for his loom and has left the door unlocked because his supper string is tied to the door-key. He is not in a fit. The lesson’s own content_html says exactly this, so the flashcards contradict the lesson.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text ch. 5: “he remembered that a piece of very fine twine was indispensable”; “He could not have locked his door without undoing his well-knotted string”.

findings.claim: Silas “is described as having ‘a strange joy’ in his face”.
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. The phrase “a strange joy” does not appear anywhere in the novel. Replaced with an unquoted statement.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text: grep for “strange joy” returns no match; “joy” never occurs in that construction.

findings.claim: A practice question, a revision tip (L5) and a paragraph of L6 give the line “There’s debts we can’t pay like money debts” to Nancy.
findings.truth: The line is Godfrey’s, spoken to Nancy in chapter 20. The L5 content_html already says so, so the unit contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text ch. 20: “‘No,’ said Godfrey … ‘there’s debts we can’t pay like money debts, by paying extra for the years that have slipped by.’”

findings.claim: Lesson 8 teaches AO4 throughout: a dedicated “AO4: Quality of Written Expression” section, a four-AO key fact, a match knowledge check pairing AO4 with “Spelling, punctuation, and grammar”, a flashcard on what AO4 rewards, the exam tip “integrates all four AOs”, and the takeaway “40 marks split equally across AO1, AO2, AO3, and AO4”.
findings.truth: Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 only. Spelling, punctuation and grammar earn no marks on the 19th-century prose question, and the spec states no equal split. Every AO4 claim corrected; the match set re-paired to AO1 / AO2 / AO3 (context).
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md — “Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.”

findings.claim: “Read an extract from Chapter 5 where Silas counts his gold by firelight.”
findings.truth: Chapter 5 is Silas’s return from the twine errand and his discovery of the theft. The gold-counting-by-night passage is chapter 2. Changed to Chapter 2.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text: ch. 2 “it was only in the night, when his work was done, that he drew them out”; ch. 5 opens “When Dunstan Cass turned his back on the cottage…” and ends with the “cry of desolation”.

findings.claim: Dunstan is “the younger son of Squire Cass” (glossary and definition), and the Squire’s “poor parenting produces two very different sons” (L1).
findings.truth: The Squire has more than two sons — Eliot names Godfrey “the eldest”, Dunstan “the second son”, and Bob Cass appears at the New Year dance. Reworded to “the second son” and “shows in two very different sons”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text ch. 3: “the courses of the second son, Dunstan”; “Mr. Godfrey, the eldest”; ch. 11: “Bob Cass was figuring in a hornpipe”.

findings.claim: Nancy is “unable to have children” and Godfrey suffers from “infertility” (definition, glossary and two flashcards).
findings.truth: The novel never says they cannot have children. Nancy speaks of “my little baby dying”, and Eliot calls the home “childless”. Reworded to “their home stays childless”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text ch. 20: “I could better have bore my little baby dying”; ch. 17: “a noble-hearted, childless woman”.

findings.claim: “Symbolism — gold/Eppie parallel, stone-pit, the stone-pit (the novel’s symbol of buried guilt).”
findings.truth: “Stone-pit” is listed twice. The third symbol the unit teaches (lesson 7) is the hearth. Corrected to gold/Eppie parallel, the hearth, and the stone-pit.
findings.evidence: Lesson 7 content_html: “Symbolism: Gold, Eppie & the Hearth”.

findings.claim: “The novel ends with Eppie and Aaron Winthrop (Dolly’s son) planning their garden together.”
findings.truth: The garden is planned in chapter 16 and is already made by the Conclusion, where Eppie and Aaron marry and walk home to it. The claim is loose rather than wrong, and the correction would ripple through narration for no mark gain.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text, Conclusion: “‘O father,’ said Eppie, ‘what a pretty home ours is!’”

findings.claim: Dunsey “kills Godfrey’s horse Wildfire in a drunken riding accident”.
findings.truth: Eliot gives him “a draught of brandy from his pocket-pistol” before the run and more brandy after the fall; he takes “one fence too many” in exasperation. “Drunken” overstates it but the recklessness is Eliot’s point, so no edit.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text ch. 4: “encouraged by confidence in his luck, and by a draught of brandy from his pocket-pistol”.

summary: Every lesson carried the wrong exam frame: the 40-mark source-based 19th-century prose question was taught as 20-mark extract questions plus a four-AO essay, with AO4 and SPaG credited throughout lesson 8. Text checks found one fabricated quotation (“a strange joy”), one misquotation (the gold as “companions”), two flashcards that put Silas in a cataleptic fit during the theft against the lesson’s own text, and Godfrey’s chapter-20 line about debts given to Nancy in three places.
